name: Bubble Sort
shortDescription: Repeatedly steps through the list, compares adjacent elements, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
detailedDescription: Bubble Sort is a foundational comparison-based sorting algorithm. In each pass through the array, adjacent elements are compared and swapped if out of order. With each pass, the extreme unsorted element bubbles to its correct position at the end of the array. An optimized version detects if no swaps occurred during a pass, terminating early in O(n) time.
recommendedUseCases: Educational demonstrations and teaching core sorting concepts
Detecting whether an array is already sorted in a single pass
Very small datasets (n < 20) where implementation simplicity is valued
advantages: Extremely simple to conceptualize and implement
Stable sorting preserves the relative order of duplicate elements
In-place sorting requiring only O(1) auxiliary memory
Best-case O(n) time complexity with the swapped flag optimization
disadvantages: O(n²) time complexity makes it impractical for large datasets
Performs excessive write operations compared to Selection Sort
Generally slower than Insertion Sort for small or nearly sorted lists
commonMistakes: Forgetting the swapped flag optimization, leading to O(n²) best-case time
Inner loop upper bound mistakes (iterating up to n-1 instead of n-i-1)
Off-by-one errors causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException when checking j + 1
examQuestions: What is the maximum number of comparisons in Bubble Sort for an array of size n? (Answer: n(n-1)/2)
Is Bubble Sort stable? Explain why adjacent element comparisons preserve stability.
Under what condition does Bubble Sort execute in O(n) time?
pseudocode:
procedure bubbleSort(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    repeat
        swapped = false
        for i = 1 to n-1 inclusive do
            if A[i-1] > A[i] then
                swap(A[i-1], A[i])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        n = n - 1
    until not swapped
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure bubbleSortDescending(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    repeat
        swapped = false
        for i = 1 to n-1 inclusive do
            if A[i-1] < A[i] then
                swap(A[i-1], A[i])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        n = n - 1
    until not swapped
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.compare: Compare adjacent elements arr[j] and arr[j+1] to check if they are in the wrong order.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: The extreme element in the current pass has settled into its final sorted position.
conceptualLineExplanations.early_exit: Zero swaps occurred in this pass, proving the array is fully sorted. We can safely terminate.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap: Swap adjacent elements since they violate the target sorting order.

name: Bucket Sort
shortDescription: Distributes elements into a number of buckets, then sorts each bucket individually.
detailedDescription: Bucket Sort is a scatter-gather sorting algorithm. It distributes the elements of an array into several dynamically sized buckets based on their values. Each bucket is subsequently sorted individually—often using Insertion Sort or recursion—and finally concatenated into the output array. When input data is uniformly distributed across a range, Bucket Sort executes in linear O(n) average time.
recommendedUseCases: Uniformly distributed floating-point or integer datasets over a known range
External sorting where buckets correspond to independent disks or nodes
Preprocessing step for parallel computing architectures
advantages: Achieves average linear O(n) time when elements are evenly distributed
Stable when underlying bucket sort is stable (e.g. insertion sort)
Easily distributed across multiple processor threads
disadvantages: Degrades to O(n²) if all elements cluster into a single bucket (skewed distribution)
Requires extra auxiliary space for bucket data structures
Inefficient when data distribution is unknown or severely clumped
commonMistakes: Assuming uniform distribution on highly clustered or skewed inputs
Bucket index calculation resulting in out-of-bounds error for maximum element
Overlooking negative integers by assuming values lie in [0, 1)
examQuestions: Under what input conditions does Bucket Sort achieve O(n) average time complexity?
What happens to the performance of Bucket Sort if all elements map to the exact same bucket?
Compare Bucket Sort with Counting Sort in terms of memory requirements for large ranges.
pseudocode:
procedure bucketSort(A, k)
    create k empty buckets
    minVal = min(A), maxVal = max(A)
    for x in A do
        insert x into bucket[floor((x - minVal) / range * (k - 1))]
    end for
    for each bucket do
        insertionSort(bucket)
    end for
    concatenate all buckets into A
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure bucketSortDescending(A, k)
    create k empty buckets
    minVal = min(A), maxVal = max(A)
    for x in A do
        insert x into bucket[floor((x - minVal) / range * (k - 1))]
    end for
    for each bucket do
        insertionSortDescending(bucket)
    end for
    concatenate buckets in reverse order into A
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.flush_bucket: Gather elements from ordered buckets back into contiguous array positions.
conceptualLineExplanations.distribute: Scatter current element into its mathematically determined bucket interval.

name: Cocktail Shaker Sort
shortDescription: A bidirectional variation of Bubble Sort that traverses the list alternating in both directions.
detailedDescription: Cocktail Shaker Sort (also called Bidirectional Bubble Sort, Ripple Sort, or Shuttle Sort) improves on standard Bubble Sort by alternating passes in both directions. In standard Bubble Sort, elements near the beginning move quickly, but elements stuck at the opposite end move forward by only one position per full pass. By sweeping backward, Cocktail Shaker Sort eliminates these in a single pass, noticeably speeding up partially ordered lists in both ascending and descending modes.
recommendedUseCases: Arrays with 'turtle' elements where small items are stuck near the end of the array
Educational comparisons illustrating bidirectional traversal benefits
Nearly sorted arrays where alternating sweeps terminate rapidly
advantages: Resolves the 'turtle problem' inherent to standard Bubble Sort
Stable: preserves the relative ordering of equal keys
In-place: requires only O(1) auxiliary memory
Best case is O(n) for already sorted arrays
disadvantages: Still suffers from O(n²) average and worst case time complexity
More complicated loop management than standard Bubble Sort
Outperformed by Insertion Sort on almost all inputs
commonMistakes: Forgetting to decrement end or increment start, causing infinite loops
Directional index boundary errors during the backward iteration
Omitting the early termination swapped flag check between half-passes
examQuestions: What is the 'turtle problem' in Bubble Sort, and how does Cocktail Shaker Sort solve it?
Is Cocktail Shaker Sort stable? Why?
What is the worst-case number of comparisons for Cocktail Shaker Sort?
pseudocode:
procedure cocktailShakerSort(A)
    start = 0, end = length(A) - 1, swapped = true
    while swapped do
        swapped = false
        for i = start to end - 1 do
            if A[i] > A[i+1] then
                swap(A[i], A[i+1])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        if not swapped then break
        end = end - 1
        for i = end - 1 down to start do
            if A[i] > A[i+1] then
                swap(A[i], A[i+1])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        start = start + 1
    end while
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure cocktailShakerSortDescending(A)
    start = 0, end = length(A) - 1, swapped = true
    while swapped do
        swapped = false
        for i = start to end - 1 do
            if A[i] < A[i+1] then
                swap(A[i], A[i+1])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        if not swapped then break
        end = end - 1
        for i = end - 1 down to start do
            if A[i] < A[i+1] then
                swap(A[i], A[i+1])
                swapped = true
            end if
        end for
        start = start + 1
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.swap_backward: Swap out-of-order adjacent elements moving backward.
conceptualLineExplanations.compare_forward: Compare adjacent elements in the forward pass.
conceptualLineExplanations.compare_backward: Compare adjacent elements in the backward pass.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap_forward: Swap out-of-order adjacent elements moving forward.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: Mark the element that has settled into its final sorted position.

name: Comb Sort
shortDescription: An improvement over Bubble Sort that uses a diminishing gap with a shrink factor of 1.3 to eliminate turtles.
detailedDescription: Comb Sort was designed in 1980 by Włodzimierz Dobosiewicz and revived by Stephen Lacey and Richard Box in 1991. Like Shell Sort does for Insertion Sort, Comb Sort improves Bubble Sort by comparing elements over an initial large gap. The gap shrinks by an empirically ideal factor of 1.3 on each iteration until it reaches 1. This rapid elimination of out-of-place values at the end of lists brings average runtime down to near O(n log n).
recommendedUseCases: Lightweight replacement for Bubble Sort when simplicity with high practical speed is required
Embedded systems where code footprint must be minimal and recursion is prohibited
Demonstrating how diminishing gap techniques transform quadratic exchange algorithms
advantages: Significantly faster than Bubble Sort in practice (approaches O(n log n) average)
Extremely simple code with zero recursion and O(1) auxiliary space
Eliminates both 'rabbits' and 'turtles' efficiently
disadvantages: Unstable: comparisons across gap intervals alter the relative ordering of duplicates
Worst case is still O(n²) for certain malicious permutations
Lacks standard library adoption compared to Quick Sort or Tim Sort
commonMistakes: Terminating before gap == 1 and swapped == false
Using an incorrect shrink factor (empirical studies prove 1.3 is optimal)
Assuming it is stable
examQuestions: Why is 1.3 considered the optimal shrink factor for Comb Sort?
How does Comb Sort compare to Shell Sort in terms of underlying mechanism?
Why does Comb Sort lose the stability that Bubble Sort possessed?
pseudocode:
procedure combSort(A)
    n = length(A)
    gap = n
    shrink = 1.3
    sorted = false
    while not sorted do
        gap = floor(gap / shrink)
        if gap <= 1 then
            gap = 1
            sorted = true
        end if
        for i = 0 to n - gap - 1 do
            if A[i] > A[i + gap] then
                swap(A[i], A[i + gap])
                sorted = false
            end if
        end for
    end while
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure combSortDescending(A)
    n = length(A)
    gap = n
    shrink = 1.3
    sorted = false
    while not sorted do
        gap = floor(gap / shrink)
        if gap <= 1 then
            gap = 1
            sorted = true
        end if
        for i = 0 to n - gap - 1 do
            if A[i] < A[i + gap] then
                swap(A[i], A[i + gap])
                sorted = false
            end if
        end for
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.compare_comb: Compare elements separated by the current shrink gap.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap_comb: Swap inverted elements across the comb gap distance.

name: Counting Sort
shortDescription: An integer sorting algorithm that operates by counting the number of objects possessing each distinct key value.
detailedDescription: Counting Sort is a non-comparison based integer sorting algorithm. Rather than comparing elements against each other, it counts the occurrences of each unique integer in a frequency array. By calculating prefix sums of these frequencies, it determines the exact final position of every element in O(n + k) time, where k is the range of inputs. This implementation includes an offset for negative integers and validates bounds to prevent memory overflow.
recommendedUseCases: Datasets with small integer ranges (k = O(n))
Subroutine inside Radix Sort (where radix digits are in range 0..9 or 0..255)
Sorting test scores, ages, or census discrete categories
advantages: Linear O(n + k) time complexity beats the theoretical O(n log n) comparison lower bound
Completely stable when implemented using cumulative prefix sum backwards iteration
Simple and predictable deterministic runtime
disadvantages: Not a comparison sort; cannot sort general objects without numeric keys
Requires excessive O(k) memory if the difference between maximum and minimum is huge (e.g., sorting [1, 10000000])
Not in-place: requires auxiliary frequency and output arrays
commonMistakes: Failing to support negative numbers by omitting the minimum offset shift
Iterating forward instead of backward when generating the output array, breaking stability
Memory exhaustion when sorting small arrays containing very large integer values
examQuestions: Why does Counting Sort violate the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts?
Under what condition does Counting Sort become slower than Quick Sort or Merge Sort? (Answer: When k >> n log n)
How does prefix sum accumulation guarantee algorithm stability?
pseudocode:
procedure countingSort(A)
    min = min(A), max = max(A)
    range = max - min + 1
    count = array of size range initialized to 0
    output = array of size length(A)

    for x in A do
        count[x - min] = count[x - min] + 1
    end for

    for i = 1 to range - 1 do
        count[i] = count[i] + count[i - 1]
    end for

    for i = length(A) - 1 down to 0 do
        val = A[i]
        output[count[val - min] - 1] = val
        count[val - min] = count[val - min] - 1
    end for

    copy output back to A
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure countingSortDescending(A)
    min = min(A), max = max(A)
    range = max - min + 1
    count = array of size range initialized to 0
    output = array of size length(A)

    for x in A do
        count[x - min] = count[x - min] + 1
    end for

    for i = range - 2 down to 0 do
        count[i] = count[i] + count[i + 1]
    end for

    for i = length(A) - 1 down to 0 do
        val = A[i]
        output[count[val - min] - 1] = val
        count[val - min] = count[val - min] - 1
    end for

    copy output back to A
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.write_output: Place the value into its exact predetermined index from the cumulative frequency map.
conceptualLineExplanations.frequency_count: Increment the tally counter for the current integer value.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: Mark the element as fixed in its final sorted position.

name: Cycle Sort
shortDescription: An in-place sorting algorithm that minimizes the number of memory writes, theoretically writing to memory at most O(n) times.
detailedDescription: Cycle Sort is based on the idea that permutations can be factored into disjoint cyclic permutations. For each element, it calculates its exact final position in the sorted array by counting how many elements are smaller (or greater for descending) than it, then deposits it there, displacing whatever element was previously residing at that slot. The displaced element is similarly routed to its correct location until the cycle completes. It is theoretically optimal in minimizing write operations.
recommendedUseCases: Flash memory, EEPROM, and SSD storage where write wear degradation is a critical concern
Embedded sensors with constrained write energy budgets
Theoretical computer science studies on minimum-write permutations
advantages: Theoretically optimal write count: each item is written at most once if already in place, or minimal cycle hops
In-place sorting requiring strictly O(1) auxiliary space
No complex data structure or recursive call stack overhead
disadvantages: O(n²) time complexity across all cases due to counting comparisons
Unstable algorithm
Complex logic to handle duplicate keys without infinite looping
commonMistakes: Infinite loops caused by duplicate elements without skipping `while (item == array[pos]) pos++`
Failing to close the cycle when pos returns to cycleStart
Confusing Cycle Sort with counting sort
examQuestions: Why is Cycle Sort optimal in terms of memory writes?
What is the maximum number of memory writes performed by Cycle Sort on an array of size n? (Answer: n - 1 writes)
How are duplicate keys handled to guarantee termination in Cycle Sort?
pseudocode:
procedure cycleSort(A)
    n = length(A)
    for cycleStart = 0 to n - 2 do
        item = A[cycleStart]
        pos = cycleStart
        for i = cycleStart + 1 to n - 1 do
            if A[i] < item then pos = pos + 1
        end for
        if pos == cycleStart then continue
        while item == A[pos] do pos = pos + 1
        swap(item, A[pos])
        while pos != cycleStart do
            pos = cycleStart
            for i = cycleStart + 1 to n - 1 do
                if A[i] < item then pos = pos + 1
            end for
            while item == A[pos] do pos = pos + 1
            swap(item, A[pos])
        end while
    end for
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure cycleSortDescending(A)
    n = length(A)
    for cycleStart = 0 to n - 2 do
        item = A[cycleStart]
        pos = cycleStart
        for i = cycleStart + 1 to n - 1 do
            if A[i] > item then pos = pos + 1
        end for
        if pos == cycleStart then continue
        while item == A[pos] do pos = pos + 1
        swap(item, A[pos])
        while pos != cycleStart do
            pos = cycleStart
            for i = cycleStart + 1 to n - 1 do
                if A[i] > item then pos = pos + 1
            end for
            while item == A[pos] do pos = pos + 1
            swap(item, A[pos])
        end while
    end for
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.already_placed: Item is confirmed already located in its target position.
conceptualLineExplanations.count_smaller: Count elements in subarray to compute target position for displaced item.
conceptualLineExplanations.start_cycle: Select origin element for current disjoint permutation cycle.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: Mark element as fixed in sorted position.
conceptualLineExplanations.write_cycle: Write displaced item directly into its mathematically determined target slot.

name: Gnome Sort
shortDescription: A delightfully simple sorting algorithm based on how a garden gnome sorts a line of flower pots.
detailedDescription: Gnome Sort (originally named 'Stupid Sort' by Hamid Sarbazi-Azad in 2000, then described by Dick Grune as Gnome Sort) is conceptually the simplest comparison sort. Imagine a garden gnome sorting flower pots: he looks at the pot next to him and the previous pot. If they are in order, he steps forward to the next pot. If out of order, he swaps them and steps one pot backward. He continues until reaching the end. It behaves like Insertion Sort implemented without nested loops.
recommendedUseCases: Teaching basic algorithm state machines without nested loop constructs
Tiny datasets or nearly-sorted lists where code simplicity is prioritized
Hardware state-machine pipelines with single-register pointer controls
advantages: Remarkably simple: uses a single index pointer and no nested loops
Stable: adjacent swaps preserve identical element order
In-place: requires strictly O(1) auxiliary space
Adaptive: runs in linear O(n) time on already sorted arrays
disadvantages: O(n²) average and worst-case time complexity
Performs many redundant single-step backwards traversals
Inferior to Insertion Sort in raw operation count on random data
commonMistakes: Failing to handle index == 0 by advancing to 1, causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (-1)
Thinking Gnome Sort requires nested loops
Using strict inequality instead of non-strict, which destroys stability
examQuestions: How is Gnome Sort conceptually related to Insertion Sort? (Answer: It performs the same element shifts, but through repeated adjacent swaps and backwards traversal)
What is the maximum number of swaps Gnome Sort performs in reverse sorted input? (Answer: n(n-1)/2)
Why does Gnome Sort execute in O(n) time for already sorted data?
pseudocode:
procedure gnomeSort(A)
    pos = 0
    while pos < length(A) do
        if pos == 0 or A[pos] >= A[pos-1] then
            pos = pos + 1
        else
            swap(A[pos], A[pos-1])
            pos = pos - 1
        end if
    end while
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure gnomeSortDescending(A)
    pos = 0
    while pos < length(A) do
        if pos == 0 or A[pos] <= A[pos-1] then
            pos = pos + 1
        else
            swap(A[pos], A[pos-1])
            pos = pos - 1
        end if
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.compare_gnome: Gnome checks if current pot is in order with the previous pot.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap_gnome: Gnome swaps the two out-of-order pots and steps one position backward.

name: Heap Sort
shortDescription: Converts the array into a Heap data structure (Max-Heap for ascending, Min-Heap for descending) and iteratively extracts root.
detailedDescription: Heap Sort uses a binary heap to manage sorting efficiently. In ascending mode, it transforms the array into a Max-Heap where each parent is >= children, repeatedly moving the max root to the end. In descending mode, it transforms the array into a Min-Heap where each parent is <= children, repeatedly moving the min root to the end. It achieves guaranteed O(n log n) runtime with strictly O(1) auxiliary space.
recommendedUseCases: Embedded and real-time systems where worst-case O(n log n) and strict O(1) memory guarantees are required
Security-critical systems seeking immunity against Quick Sort's worst-case O(n²) denial-of-service vulnerabilities
Priority queues and top-K elements selection
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time without recursion or extra memory
In-place sorting requiring strictly O(1) auxiliary space
Immune to quadratic worst-case degradation seen in Quick Sort
disadvantages: Poor cache locality: jumping between parent 2i+1 and 2i+2 leads to frequent cache misses
Unstable: heap structure swaps do not preserve relative order of duplicates
Slower in practice on modern CPUs than Quick Sort and Merge Sort due to memory access patterns
commonMistakes: Calculating parent/child indices incorrectly (off-by-one with 2*i + 1 vs 2*i + 2)
Starting build-heap from 0 instead of n/2 - 1
Forgetting to pass reduced heap size n into heapify during extraction phase
examQuestions: Why does building a binary heap take O(n) time instead of O(n log n)?
Compare Heap Sort with Quick Sort in terms of cache performance and memory locality.
Why is Heap Sort unstable? Give a simple counterexample.
pseudocode:
procedure heapSort(A)
    n = length(A)
    for i = floor(n/2) - 1 down to 0 do
        heapify(A, n, i)
    end for
    for i = n - 1 down to 1 do
        swap(A[0], A[i])
        heapify(A, i, 0)
    end for
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure heapSortDescending(A)
    n = length(A)
    for i = floor(n/2) - 1 down to 0 do
        minHeapify(A, n, i)
    end for
    for i = n - 1 down to 1 do
        swap(A[0], A[i])
        minHeapify(A, i, 0)
    end for
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.sift_down: Sift down the violation to restore heap structural invariants.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap_root: Move root element to its final sorted location at end of unsorted boundary.
conceptualLineExplanations.extract_root: Locate root element containing extremum value of current active heap.
conceptualLineExplanations.compare_child: Compare parent node with its left and right children.

name: Insertion Sort
shortDescription: Builds the final sorted array one item at a time by repeatedly inserting each new element into its proper position.
detailedDescription: Insertion Sort mimics the way people naturally sort playing cards in their hands. It iterates through the array, taking each element as a 'key', and shifts all out-of-order elements in the sorted sublist to the right to make room for insertion. It is remarkably efficient for small arrays (typically n < 32) and nearly-sorted arrays, making it an essential building block inside advanced hybrid algorithms like Tim Sort and Introsort.
recommendedUseCases: Small datasets (n < 32) where low overhead beats O(n log n) recursive algorithms
Subarrays inside hybrid algorithms like Tim Sort and Quick Sort / Introsort
Nearly sorted or partially sorted datasets (runs in near O(n) time)
Online sorting where data arrives continuously in a stream
advantages: Adaptive: runs in O(n) time when array is already sorted or nearly sorted
Stable: preserves the relative ordering of duplicate elements
In-place: requires only O(1) auxiliary memory
Online: can sort a list as it receives it element by element
disadvantages: O(n²) worst and average case makes it impractical for large datasets
Performs many data shift operations when elements are far from target positions
commonMistakes: Off-by-one errors with index j when shifting elements
Forgetting to check j >= 0 before accessing array[j], causing IndexOutOfBounds
Using swap instead of direct shifts, introducing unnecessary writes
examQuestions: What is the number of comparisons in Insertion Sort when the input is already sorted? (Answer: n - 1)
How does Insertion Sort compare to Bubble Sort for nearly sorted arrays? (Answer: Both are O(n), but Insertion Sort does fewer operations and no swaps)
Explain why Tim Sort uses Insertion Sort for small runs.
pseudocode:
procedure insertionSort(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 1 to n-1 do
        key = A[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and A[j] > key do
            A[j+1] = A[j]
            j = j - 1
        end while
        A[j+1] = key
    end for
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure insertionSortDescending(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 1 to n-1 do
        key = A[i]
        j = i - 1
        while j >= 0 and A[j] < key do
            A[j+1] = A[j]
            j = j - 1
        end while
        A[j+1] = key
    end for
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.pick_key: Select the current element as the 'key' to be inserted into the sorted subarray.
conceptualLineExplanations.compare: Compare the key with the sorted element to check if shifting is required.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_prefix: The prefix up to this index is now verified to be sorted.
conceptualLineExplanations.shift: Shift the out-of-order sorted element one position to the right.
conceptualLineExplanations.insert_key: Drop the key into the vacant position that maintains sorted order.

name: Merge Sort
shortDescription: Divides the array into two halves, recursively sorts them, and merges the two sorted halves.
detailedDescription: Merge Sort was invented by John von Neumann in 1945. It follows the Divide and Conquer paradigm: it recursively breaks the input list into two equal halves until reaching single-element subarrays (which are inherently sorted), and then merges them back together in linear time. Because its worst-case performance is guaranteed to be O(n log n) and it is completely stable, Merge Sort is heavily used for sorting linked lists, external datasets, and general object collections.
recommendedUseCases: Sorting linked lists (merging does not require random array indexing or extra space)
External sorting for massive datasets that cannot fit entirely in RAM
When guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time is critical without variance
Sorting objects where preserving the relative order of equal keys (stability) is mandatory
advantages: Guaranteed O(n log n) performance across best, average, and worst cases
Completely stable sorting algorithm
Highly parallelizable divide-and-conquer structure
Optimal for sequential data structures like linked lists
disadvantages: Requires O(n) auxiliary memory for merging arrays
Higher constant factor overhead than Quick Sort for standard in-memory arrays
Recursion stack overhead O(log n)
commonMistakes: Integer overflow when computing mid = (left + right) / 2 instead of left + (right - left) / 2
Violating stability by using `<` instead of `<=` when comparing L[i] and R[j]
Forgetting to flush remaining elements from the left or right sub-arrays
examQuestions: State the recurrence relation for Merge Sort and solve it using Master Theorem. (T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) => O(n log n))
Why is Merge Sort preferred over Quick Sort for sorting Linked Lists?
How can Merge Sort be modified to count inversions in an array in O(n log n) time?
pseudocode:
procedure mergeSort(A, left, right)
    if left < right then
        mid = left + (right - left) / 2
        mergeSort(A, left, mid)
        mergeSort(A, mid + 1, right)
        merge(A, left, mid, right)
    end if
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure mergeSortDescending(A, left, right)
    if left < right then
        mid = left + (right - left) / 2
        mergeSortDescending(A, left, mid)
        mergeSortDescending(A, mid + 1, right)
        mergeDescending(A, left, mid, right)
    end if
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.compare_merge: Compare elements from heads of both sorted sublists.
conceptualLineExplanations.merge_start: Allocate temporary storage and begin the linear merge process.
conceptualLineExplanations.merge_complete: The merged subarray is now fully ordered.
conceptualLineExplanations.divide: Divide the current subarray at midpoint into left and right sub-problems.
conceptualLineExplanations.write_merge: Write the selected element into the target array position.

name: Pigeonhole Sort
shortDescription: Places each element into a dedicated 'hole' indexed by its key, then iterates sequentially through the holes.
detailedDescription: Pigeonhole Sort is a distribution sorting algorithm suitable when the number of elements (n) and the range of possible key values (Range) are approximately equal. Based on the Dirichlet Drawer / Pigeonhole Principle, it assigns each item to a pigeonhole labeled with its value. Once all items are pigeonholed, it visits each hole in ascending order (or descending order from highest to lowest) to reconstruct the fully sorted array. It preserves stability and handles negative values via minimum offsets.
recommendedUseCases: Sorting keys where range is close to the number of elements n
Demonstrating the Pigeonhole Principle in algorithmic computer science
Direct key indexing without comparison logic
advantages: Linear O(n + Range) time complexity
Completely stable: preserves original order of duplicates within each hole
Very simple to visualize and comprehend
disadvantages: Excessive memory consumption if Range is significantly larger than n
Restricted to integer keys or discrete mappable values
Not in-place: requires lists of pigeonholes
commonMistakes: Allocating huge arrays when input numbers have large gaps (e.g., [1, 1000000])
Confusing Pigeonhole Sort with Counting Sort (Counting Sort stores counts; Pigeonhole stores actual elements/lists)
Index calculation errors without subtracting the minimum value
examQuestions: What is the key difference between Pigeonhole Sort and Counting Sort?
What is the Pigeonhole Principle, and how does it relate to duplicate keys?
Under what conditions does Pigeonhole Sort become impractical?
pseudocode:
procedure pigeonholeSort(A)
    min = min(A), max = max(A)
    range = max - min + 1
    create array of empty lists 'holes' of size range
    for x in A do
        holes[x - min].append(x)
    end for
    index = 0
    for hole in holes do
        for x in hole do
            A[index] = x
            index = index + 1
        end for
    end for
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure pigeonholeSortDescending(A)
    min = min(A), max = max(A)
    range = max - min + 1
    create array of empty lists 'holes' of size range
    for x in A do
        holes[x - min].append(x)
    end for
    index = 0
    for count from range - 1 down to 0 do
        for x in holes[count] do
            A[index] = x
            index = index + 1
        end for
    end for
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.retrieve_hole: Extract elements sequentially from pigeonholes back to the array.
conceptualLineExplanations.put_hole: Deposit element into its dedicated value-indexed pigeonhole.

name: Quick Sort
shortDescription: Picks an element as pivot and partitions the given array around the picked pivot.
detailedDescription: Quick Sort, developed by Tony Hoare in 1959, is one of the most widely used general-purpose sorting algorithms. It works by choosing a 'pivot' element, rearranging the array so that elements matching the target order relative to the pivot appear before it and remaining elements appear after it (partitioning), and then recursively sorting the left and right partitions. Because it sorts in-place and exhibits superb cache locality, its constant factors are exceptionally small.
recommendedUseCases: Standard general-purpose in-memory sorting of primitive types (e.g. Arrays.sort in Java uses Dual-Pivot Quicksort)
Systems with fast cache hierarchies benefiting from sequential memory locality
When in-place sorting is required and average O(n log n) performance is needed
advantages: Very fast practical runtime due to excellent cache locality and low constant factors
In-place sorting requiring only O(log n) stack memory
Easily adaptable to Randomized Pivot or Dual-Pivot strategies
disadvantages: Worst-case O(n²) time complexity if poor pivots (e.g., already sorted array with naive pivot) are chosen
Unstable algorithm: relative order of equal keys is not preserved
Recursive call stack can reach O(n) depth in worst case without tail call optimization
commonMistakes: Picking a fixed pivot (e.g., always last element) on already sorted arrays triggering O(n²)
Lomuto partition indexing bugs with the i and j pointer increments
Stack overflow from deep recursion on unbalanced partitions
examQuestions: What causes Quick Sort to degrade to O(n²) time complexity, and how can randomized pivot or 3-way partitioning prevent it?
Compare Quick Sort and Merge Sort regarding auxiliary space, stability, and cache performance.
Explain Lomuto partitioning vs Hoare partitioning. Which performs fewer swaps?
pseudocode:
procedure quickSort(A, low, high)
    if low < high then
        pi = partition(A, low, high)
        quickSort(A, low, pi - 1)
        quickSort(A, pi + 1, high)
    end if
end procedure

procedure partition(A, low, high)
    pivot = A[high]
    i = low - 1
    for j = low to high - 1 do
        if A[j] <= pivot then
            i = i + 1
            swap(A[i], A[j])
        end if
    end for
    swap(A[i + 1], A[high])
    return i + 1
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure quickSortDescending(A, low, high)
    if low < high then
        pi = partitionDescending(A, low, high)
        quickSortDescending(A, low, pi - 1)
        quickSortDescending(A, pi + 1, high)
    end if
end procedure

procedure partitionDescending(A, low, high)
    pivot = A[high]
    i = low - 1
    for j = low to high - 1 do
        if A[j] >= pivot then
            i = i + 1
            swap(A[i], A[j])
        end if
    end for
    swap(A[i + 1], A[high])
    return i + 1
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.swap_smaller: Swap element into target partition boundary.
conceptualLineExplanations.choose_pivot: Select the pivot element against which all other subarray elements are compared.
conceptualLineExplanations.partition_start: Define active subarray boundary and prepare partition pointers.
conceptualLineExplanations.place_pivot: Swap pivot into its permanent position between partitions.
conceptualLineExplanations.pivot_placed: Pivot element is now fixed in its final sorted index.

name: Radix Sort
shortDescription: Sorts numbers by processing individual digits, either from least significant digit (LSD) or most significant digit (MSD).
detailedDescription: Radix Sort sorts integer data by distributing elements into buckets according to their individual radix digits, beginning at the Least Significant Digit (LSD) and progressing to the Most Significant Digit (MSD). At each digit position, a stable sorting algorithm (typically Counting Sort) sorts the elements. By chaining stable passes, earlier sorted digits maintain their order. This implementation segregates negative numbers to seamlessly support all signed 32-bit integers in both ascending and descending modes.
recommendedUseCases: Sorting large collections of fixed-length integers or fixed-width strings
Card sorting machines (historical origin of the algorithm)
When data key length d is much smaller than log(n)
advantages: Linear O(d(n + k)) time complexity when key length d is constant
Completely stable sorting preserves original order of identical keys
Avoids comparison operations altogether
disadvantages: Not in-place: requires O(n + k) auxiliary memory for output and bucket storage
Significant constant factors can make it slower than Quick Sort for small/medium arrays
Tied to fixed-width integer or string keys; less flexible for arbitrary data types
commonMistakes: Omitting support for negative numbers, corrupting order of signed integer inputs
Iterating digits from MSD to LSD without recursion, destroying sorted lower digits
Using an unstable sub-sorting method for individual digit passes
examQuestions: What is the difference between LSD (Least Significant Digit) and MSD (Most Significant Digit) Radix Sort?
Under what mathematical conditions will Radix Sort execute faster than an optimal comparison sort?
How does Radix Sort preserve stability across multiple digit passes?
pseudocode:
procedure radixSort(A)
    maxVal = max(A)
    exp = 1
    while maxVal / exp > 0 do
        countingSortByDigit(A, exp)
        exp = exp * 10
    end while
end procedure
pythonCode:
def radix_sort(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    if len(arr) <= 1:
        return arr
    positives = [x for x in arr if x >= 0]
    negatives = [-x for x in arr if x < 0]

    def lsd_sort(a: list[int]) -> list[int]:
        if not a:
            return a
        max_val = max(a)
        exp = 1
        while max_val // exp > 0:
            count = [0] * 10
            out = [0] * len(a)
            for x in a:
                count[(x // exp) % 10] += 1
            for i in range(1, 10):
                count[i] += count[i - 1]
            for i in range(len(a) - 1, -1, -1):
                d = (a[i] // exp) % 10
                out[count[d] - 1] = a[i]
                count[d] -= 1
            a = out
            exp *= 10
        return a

    sorted_pos = lsd_sort(positives)
    sorted_neg = lsd_sort(negatives)
    return [-x for x in reversed(sorted_neg)] + sorted_pos
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure radixSortDescending(A)
    maxVal = max(A)
    exp = 1
    while maxVal / exp > 0 do
        countingSortByDigitDescending(A, exp)
        exp = exp * 10
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: Mark element as fixed in sorted position.
conceptualLineExplanations.write_combined: Reassemble element into final array position.

name: Selection Sort
shortDescription: Repeatedly finds the target extremum (minimum in ascending, maximum in descending) and moves it to the front.
detailedDescription: Selection Sort divides the array into a sorted sublist at the front and an unsorted sublist at the back. It scans the unsorted portion to locate the target extremum (minimum for ascending, maximum for descending), swaps it with the leftmost unsorted element, and extends the sorted boundary by one. Because it performs at most n-1 swaps regardless of input, it is useful when write operations are significantly more expensive than reads (e.g. Flash EEPROM memory).
recommendedUseCases: Systems where memory write operations are extremely costly (e.g., EEPROM, flash)
Small lists where algorithm simplicity is paramount
Educational comparisons demonstrating the distinction between comparisons and swaps
advantages: Minimal write operations: strictly at most O(n) swaps
Simple and straightforward logic
In-place sorting with O(1) auxiliary memory
Consistent performance regardless of initial element ordering
disadvantages: O(n²) time complexity across all cases, even when array is already sorted
Not stable in standard array implementations (can jump duplicates over equal items)
Inefficient for medium to large datasets
commonMistakes: Assuming it is stable (standard array swap can alter order of identical keys)
Thinking best case is O(n); it must always scan all remaining items to verify minimum/maximum
Not checking if extremumIdx == i before swapping, generating redundant swap operations
examQuestions: Why is Selection Sort unstable? Provide an example array that demonstrates this. (e.g. [5a, 5b, 2] -> 2 swaps with 5a, putting 5a after 5b)
What is the exact number of comparisons performed by Selection Sort for array size n? (Answer: n(n-1)/2)
In what hardware scenario might Selection Sort outperform Quick Sort or Insertion Sort? (Answer: When write operations degrade hardware, like Flash memory)
pseudocode:
procedure selectionSort(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 0 to n-2 do
        minIdx = i
        for j = i+1 to n-1 do
            if A[j] < A[minIdx] then
                minIdx = j
            end if
        end for
        if minIdx != i then
            swap(A[i], A[minIdx])
        end if
    end for
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure selectionSortDescending(A : list of sortable items)
    n = length(A)
    for i = 0 to n-2 do
        maxIdx = i
        for j = i+1 to n-1 do
            if A[j] > A[maxIdx] then
                maxIdx = j
            end if
        end for
        if maxIdx != i then
            swap(A[i], A[maxIdx])
        end if
    end for
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.find_min: Assume the first element of the unsorted partition is the current extremum.
conceptualLineExplanations.new_min: Update the extremum index to the newly discovered value.
conceptualLineExplanations.swap: Swap the located extremum element into the sorted partition boundary.
conceptualLineExplanations.mark_sorted: Expand the boundary of the sorted partition by one element.

name: Shell Sort
shortDescription: An optimization over insertion sort that allows the exchange of far-apart elements using diminishing gaps.
detailedDescription: Invented by Donald Shell in 1959, Shell Sort was the first algorithm to break the O(n²) barrier for general comparison sorting. It improves upon Insertion Sort by comparing and shifting elements separated by a gap of several positions, rather than just adjacent elements. By progressively reducing the gap down to 1, distant inversions are resolved rapidly with few shifts, leaving the array nearly sorted for the final standard insertion pass.
recommendedUseCases: Medium-sized arrays where recursion stack overhead of Quick Sort or Merge Sort is unwanted
Embedded microcontrollers with severely restricted RAM and stack limits
Hardware-level sorting implementations
advantages: Significantly faster than standard Insertion Sort without requiring recursion
In-place sorting requiring strictly O(1) auxiliary space
Simple to implement compared to Heap Sort or Quick Sort
disadvantages: Unstable: jumps elements over each other, disrupting initial duplicate order
Complexity heavily depends on the chosen gap sequence (Shell, Sedgewick, Knuth, Hibbard)
Slower than modern O(n log n) algorithms for large inputs
commonMistakes: Using an inefficient gap sequence that yields O(n²) worst-case behavior
Off-by-one errors with gap termination condition (must finish with gap = 1)
Thinking Shell Sort is stable
examQuestions: How does Shell Sort overcome the fundamental limitation of Bubble and Insertion Sort? (Answer: Eliminates distant inversions in O(1) swaps)
What is the effect of using Knuth's sequence (h = 3h + 1) versus Shell's original sequence (n/2)?
Is Shell Sort an adaptive sorting algorithm?
pseudocode:
procedure shellSort(A)
    n = length(A)
    gap = floor(n/2)
    while gap > 0 do
        for i = gap to n-1 do
            temp = A[i]
            j = i
            while j >= gap and A[j - gap] > temp do
                A[j] = A[j - gap]
                j = j - gap
            end while
            A[j] = temp
        end for
        gap = floor(gap / 2)
    end while
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure shellSortDescending(A)
    n = length(A)
    gap = floor(n/2)
    while gap > 0 do
        for i = gap to n-1 do
            temp = A[i]
            j = i
            while j >= gap and A[j - gap] < temp do
                A[j] = A[j - gap]
                j = j - gap
            end while
            A[j] = temp
        end for
        gap = floor(gap / 2)
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.compare_gap: Compare element with its gap-distance predecessor.
conceptualLineExplanations.place_element: Place current element into resolved gap position.
conceptualLineExplanations.pick_element: Pick element to insert into its interleaved gap-spaced subarray.
conceptualLineExplanations.shift_gap: Shift predecessor forward by gap distance.

name: Tim Sort
shortDescription: A hybrid, stable sorting algorithm derived from Merge Sort and Insertion Sort, designed to perform exceptionally well on real-world data.
detailedDescription: Created by Tim Peters in 2002 for the Python language and subsequently adopted as the default sorting algorithm for non-primitive objects in Java (Arrays.sort and Collections.sort) and Android. Tim Sort recognizes that real-world datasets frequently contain preexisting ascending or descending sequences ('natural runs'). It detects these runs, extends short runs up to a minimum threshold ('minRun') using Insertion Sort, and merges runs hierarchically using a stack, achieving O(n) performance on partially ordered data.
recommendedUseCases: Default general-purpose sorting for Java Objects (Arrays.sort(Object[]), Collections.sort())
Default sorting engine in Python (list.sort() and sorted())
Real-world data containing preexisting sorted clusters or streaks
Systems where stability and guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case time are non-negotiable
advantages: Outstanding real-world performance by exploiting natural data order
Adaptive O(n) best-case execution on already sorted or nearly sorted lists
Completely stable: equal elements preserve original sequence
Guaranteed O(n log n) worst-case upper bound
disadvantages: Complex implementation with intricate run stack invariants
Requires auxiliary memory buffer (O(n) worst case) for merging
Higher constant overhead than Quick Sort on purely randomized primitive data
commonMistakes: Famous historic bug in the original Tim Sort run-stack collapse invariant that took over a decade to discover via formal verification
Reversing descending runs without preserving stability if non-strict inequality is used
Failing to calculate minRun such that n/minRun is close to a power of 2
examQuestions: Why is Tim Sort the default sorting algorithm for Java objects but not for primitive arrays? (Answer: Objects require stability; primitives use Dual-Pivot QuickSort)
What is a 'natural run' in Tim Sort, and how are descending runs handled?
How does Tim Sort balance runs using the stack invariant to ensure O(n log n) merge efficiency?
pseudocode:
procedure timSort(A)
    n = length(A)
    minRun = calculateMinRun(n)
    for i = 0 to n-1 step minRun do
        insertionSort(A, i, min(i + minRun - 1, n - 1))
    end for
    size = minRun
    while size < n do
        for left = 0 to n - 1 step 2 * size do
            mid = left + size - 1
            right = min(left + 2 * size - 1, n - 1)
            if mid < right then
                merge(A, left, mid, right)
            end if
        end for
        size = 2 * size
    end while
end procedure
pseudocodeDescending:
procedure timSortDescending(A)
    n = length(A)
    minRun = calculateMinRun(n)
    for i = 0 to n-1 step minRun do
        insertionSortDescending(A, i, min(i + minRun - 1, n - 1))
    end for
    size = minRun
    while size < n do
        for left = 0 to n - 1 step 2 * size do
            mid = left + size - 1
            right = min(left + 2 * size - 1, n - 1)
            if mid < right then
                mergeDescending(A, left, mid, right)
            end if
        end for
        size = 2 * size
    end while
end procedure

conceptualLineExplanations.reverse_run: Reverse strictly decreasing natural runs to ascending order.
conceptualLineExplanations.insertion_place: Use insertion sort to extend runs that are smaller than minRun.
conceptualLineExplanations.merge_runs: Merge adjacent runs together stably into a single ordered run.
